text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 § 5.2.4 — Unambiguity (Clarity): Can the requirement be understood in only one reasonable way? A requirement must be precise, concise, and have only one reasonable interpretation. Avoid subjective words such as 'user-friendly', 'fast', 'efficient', 'flexible', 'secure', 'robust', or 'appropriate'. Avoid undefined actors ('the user', 'the administrator') or unclear conditions ('when necessary', 'if possible'). Avoid compound sentences bundling multiple obligations. Template: When <trigger>, <actor> shall <action> <output> within <measurable constraint>.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 § 5.2.5 — Completeness: Does the requirement contain all necessary conditions, inputs, outputs, constraints, and exceptions without unstated assumptions? A complete requirement includes: (1) Actor: who performs or receives action, (2) Trigger or precondition: when behavior occurs, (3) Action: what the system must do, (4) Input data: information needed, (5) Output or result: what happens afterward, (6) Constraints: performance/security/business rules, and (7) Exception behavior: normal path and failure path.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 § 5.2.7 — Verifiability (Testability): Can satisfaction or violation of the requirement be objectively determined? A requirement must contain observable conditions and measurable criteria verifiable by Inspection, Analysis, Demonstration, or Test. Subjective statements like 'The app shall be easy to use' cannot be objectively verified. Quantify criteria with numeric bounds (e.g. latency, throughput, percentages, exact error states).

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 § 5.2.6 — Consistency: Does the requirement contradict other requirements, constraints, business rules, or system behavior? Requirements must be compatible in permissions, data definitions, and lifecycle states. If surrounding requirements are not available, Consistency should be marked 'Cannot Assess' unless an internal self-contradiction is present.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 § 5.2.8 — Traceability: Can the requirement be linked backward to its origin and forward to design, implementation, verification, or test artifacts? A requirement must have a unique ID (e.g. REQ-PAY-021), a valid backward source link (e.g. Stakeholder Need STK-xxx or Business Rule BR-xxx), and a downstream verification link (e.g. Test Case TC-xxx or Design DES-xxx). If only an ID exists without links, score is 1.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 § 5.2.2 — Correctness: Does the requirement accurately represent the stakeholder need, business rule, domain rule, or system constraint? A requirement is incorrect if it contradicts domain rules, standard security baselines (e.g. storing plain text passwords), or regulatory obligations. When no source document or baseline is available, Correctness is marked 'Cannot Assess'.

SMART — Specific: Targets one well-defined behavior with an explicit actor, trigger, and action, not a vague aspiration. Example: 'When a customer submits a search request, the system shall display the first 20 matching products within 2 seconds.'
SMART — Measurable: Contains concrete observable conditions: a time limit, a count, a percentage, or an explicit pass/fail check.
SMART — Time-bound: Explicitly specifies latency thresholds, response times, token validity durations, or timeout limits.
